title: The Educated Barbarian: An introduction to Stoicism (Enchiridion analysis part. 6)
summary: Final episode of NH's reading of Epictetus' Enchiridion. He covers mental self-ownership, embracing struggle as an athlete or lifter does, treating events as neutral, prescribing your own character, speaking little, avoiding bad company, delaying pleasure, and never calling yourself a philosopher. Seneca's On the Happy Life comes next, and Jungian shadow work later.
claims: Letting someone else's words control your feelings is as shameful as handing them your body, and owning your mind is worse because it governs everything
Epictetus' athlete passage describes lifting: strict regimen, injuries and defeats are the price, and people who complain about the struggle behave like children
People who resent struggle would simply stay idle with more free time; limited time makes it easier to pursue a passion
Accepting responsibility is what makes you an adult
A biological father is not the same as a dad who raises you; you owe no submission to a bad or abusive parent
Epictetus uses the gods for practical ends: assume everything happens for a reason so you never blame externals and you keep control of your response
Events are neutral; whether they are good or bad depends on interpretation, so it is up to you to use them well
Decide on the character traits you want and practice them both alone and in public; character is built by effort after a decision
Speak little: people who say few words get listened to and are more pleasant company
Don't try to fix stupid people; avoid bad company, which drags you down, and it is better to be alone
Sex within a committed relationship strengthens you while casual hookups damage you; NH ranks masturbation, casual sex and bonded sex as three levels
Don't preach about abstaining or boast about your restraint; do it for yourself
When a pleasure tempts you, delay it and picture the regret afterwards; for a junk-food craving, wait about 15 minutes to break the addiction
People dislike others based on emotion first and facts second; if they are wrong, they are the ones who lose
Don't go looking for people's flaws; judge them in neutral, factual language
Never call yourself a philosopher or a stoic; study philosophy to improve, not to impress
Don't announce your discipline or practice; let it show through how you live
The philosopher expects all harm and benefit from himself and watches himself like an enemy in ambush, which NH links to the Jungian shadow work he will cover next
